newsitem.title: FRANCE: GSM mobile phone market seen set for growth surge.
newsitem.headline: GSM mobile phone market seen set for growth surge.

text.p: The market for GSM digital mobile telephones is set for a surge in growth but competition between operators and equipment manufacturers will be merciless, industry sources say.

"A lot of people say that GSM is just mobile telecommunications. But they are wrong. It is the telecommunications of the future," an industry consultant said at the GSM World Congress, which started on Wednesday.

GSM, Global System for Mobile telecommunications, began as a European grouping trying to get common standards in many countries for digital mobile communications. The United States and Japan have their own versions as well.
But it is rapidly turning into what its ambitious name suggests -- a global standard.
Technically there are still many differences, especially in the frequencies used for the radio link.
But according to officials at Motorola Inc, these differences will soon melt away as new chipsets allow mobile phones to interact with any frequency.
The market for GSM phones, according to data by market researchers Dataquest, is set to rise to 45 to 50 million users in 1997 from 22.3 million in 1996 and 10.8 million in 1995.
DAMPS (Digital Advanced Mobile Phone Service) will reach five to seven million users in 1997, up from 3.2 million in 1996 and 1.6 million in 1995.

PDC (Japan's Pacific Digital Cellular) is set to grow to 11 to 13 million users in 1997 from 10.5 million in 1996 and three million in 1995, while CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access) will attract only 1.5-2.5 million users in 1997 versus 800,000 in 1996 and 200,000 in 1995.

The key to growth will remain professional users but mobile telecommunications is starting to turn into a mass market and lower phone prices and cuts in call rates are expected to boost this trend, industry sources say.
So in their search for market share, companies are looking at additional services to go along with the phone, such as Internet access or special dialling codes.
"1997 is going to be the year of value added services," said Alain Bravo, president of the mobile communications division of Alcatel Alsthom.

Sweden's LM Ericsson AB, Motorola and Alcatel are all developing services that will link mobile phones to a company's internal telecommunications system -- allowing a user to dial extension numbers or short dialling codes as if he or she were using a telephone in the office.
Another approach is to link mobile phones to third parties with a "loyalty factor". This would link them to a bank, retailer, airline or car rental company -- or a combination.
Already operators are experimenting with offering weather information, restaurant booking, travel updates and other services to the basic portable telephone.
And there is a move towards miniaturisation with Ericsson unveiling the smallest phone and Alcatel launching the flattest phone -- all aimed at making the portable less conspicious.
The GSM World Congress, which will last for three days in this Mediterranean resort, will be attended by more than 850 operators from around 72 countries.
